newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zairean youths queue to join rebel army in Kindu.
newsitem.headline: Zairean youths queue to join rebel army in Kindu.

text.p: Rebels on Thursday turned away youths lining up in the eastern Zairean town of Kindu to enlist in forces closing in on the northeastern capital of Kisangani.

The rebels of Laurent Kabila's Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire (ADFL) also put on display four former Rwandan Hutu soldiers who said they had fought alongside Zaire's government troops.
Would-be recruits turning up at rebel posts in Kindu, which fell to the rebels on Sunday, were told to leave their names and return when a recruitment programme was organised locally.
"It is in my interest to join the alliance and save the country," said mechanic Shungu Weilo, 22, referring to the rebel Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo -Zaire (AFDL).
Kindu, on the western bank of the rust Zaire river, is the westernmost town seized by the rebels who have seized a stretch of the east 1,000 km (600 miles) long since October.
Efforts by foreign mercenaries to bolster the ramshackle army of President Mobutu Sese Seko have failed because of poor logistics, training and morale among troops paid less than a dollar a month.
In contrast, rebel ranks have been swollen by thousands of youths from captured areas who scent victory and opportunity with the northwest capital of Kisangani in the rebel sights.
Thousands of young men paraded in eastern border towns and cities last month after training before heading for the front.
"I can't say I think all those coming forward are suitable, either physically or in their motives, but after training and education plenty will still be able to do the work," a rebel officer said.
New recruits also offer some ethnic diversity to a force which has as its shock troops mostly ethnic Tutsis, locally known as Banyamulenge who spearheaded the rebellion in the east.
With origins in Rwanda generations ago, the Tutsis rebelled when threatened with expulsion from Zaire or being hunted down by civilians in a witch-hunt encouraged by local authorities.
"The Banyamulenge are our brothers, they have liberated us and now it is our job to help them free the whole country," said Komanda Munatobina, a 20-year-old-student, at a rebel post in KIndu.
Kinshasa accuses neighbouring Rwanda, Uganda and Burundi of sending their own troops to fight alongside the rebels. The accusations are denied by all three countries and the AFDL.

The rebels put on display Rwandan Hutu soldiers from the country's ousted army. Dressed in ragged clothes and scraps of military khaki the four told reporters they surrendered in Kindu on Wednesday, three days after it fell to the ADFL.

"Me and my colleagues did not take part in the battle for Kindu. We wandered through the forest after being driven out and did not know who we would find in Kindu when we got here," said Bazirasa Anani, a corporal in the Rwandan army since 1994.
He said he had fled the rebel advance westwards to a succession of refugee camps until arriving at Lubile, 120 km (75 miles) east of Kindu in February.
"Zaire army officers gave us guns...they told us we had to fight for Zaire because the Zaireans gave us refuge when we ran away from Rwanda in 1994," Bazarisa said.
"But Kabila's soldiers have better morale and equipment..."
Over a million Rwandans, mostly of the Hutu ethnic majority, fled their homes in 1994 fearing reprisals after the genocide of 800,000 Tutsis and moderate Hutus.
"Now we want to go home to Rwanda if they will repatriate us. I have nothing to fear in Rwanda because I did not do anything in 1994 except fight as a soldier," Bazarisa said.
